content: 1. As part of the Telehealth Wheelchair Assessment Service (TWAS), 6% of respondents reported that a request for a specific service had been denied. However, most individuals ultimately received the services they needed, even if they had to pay for them out of pocket. 2. The majority of adults with spinal cord injuries (SCI) expressed satisfaction with the services provided by the Dutch service delivery system. These services included domestic and car adaptations based on medical assessments and the provision of adaptive equipment. 3. Complaints were raised regarding the treatment of participants, particularly by professionals from the Joint Medical Service. Additional concerns included the involvement of multiple organizations and officials, as well as the lengthy time required to complete these procedures. 4. In a study on wheelchair selection, 86% of participants (49 individuals) were satisfied with the process. Those supported by non-medical professionals (63%) felt more included in the selection process compared to those supported by medical staff. 5. Most participants (58%) received wheelchair education and skills training lasting less than 15 minutes. A smaller number received training lasting 15–60 minutes (12 participants) or more than one hour (7 participants). Non-medical professionals generally spent more time (30–60 minutes) on these processes compared to medical professionals, who mostly spent less than 15 minutes. 6. Regarding the fitting process, 38 out of 44 participants were satisfied. However, 78% of participants had to repair their wheelchairs, with most repairs performed by laypersons (54 cases) rather than non-medical professionals (28 cases). Despite this, 79% of participants were satisfied with the repairs. 7. Members of the Croatian Paraplegic and Tetraplegic Alliance were generally satisfied with the comprehensive wheelchair services provided to them. 8. In a survey conducted by Suzuki, Lockert, and Braun (2000), all 25 respondents (100%) stated they would recommend the seating clinic to other wheelchair users. Positive feedback highlighted the kindness and competence of therapists, the assessment process, and learning new ways to operate equipment for improved mobility. 9. Some participants suggested improvements, such as better follow-up by vendors and clinics after equipment delivery. The Honolulu Wheelchair Seating Clinic at REHAB received positive feedback, with additional recommendations for service enhancement. 10. In a study by Gowran et al. (2020), long waiting times and cancellations were identified as major concerns in Irish wheelchair services. The ad hoc and non-uniform nature of these services, along with limited education and training, led to dissatisfaction among wheelchair users. 11. Some participants described the impact of inadequate wheelchair services as a human rights issue, criticizing the Health Service Executive (HSE) for removing power, choice, and control from individuals who should have gained independence through these services. 12. The WHO 8-step wheelchair service provision model significantly improved satisfaction with mobility among children and adults. However, it did not contribute to improved mobility for children in the waitlist group. 13. Participants in the CIR Whirlwind project reported improved wheelchair skills over 10 weeks, including balancing, navigating inclines, and traveling up and down steps. However, no significant changes were observed in daily activity distances. 14. Feedback on wheelchair design highlighted issues such as the lack of clothing guards, small push rim diameters, insufficient back support, and difficulties traveling over gravel. Despite these concerns, the adjustable wheelchair provided by the CIR Whirlwind project received favorable feedback. 15. In a study by Williams et al. (2017), participants noted difficulties obtaining replacement parts and expressed frustration with poorly made or non-functional wheelchairs. Preferences for tire types (inflatable vs. solid rubber) were also highlighted. 16. The WHO 2008 Guidelines on wheelchair service provision were found to improve satisfaction with most services, except for follow-up services among adults and training in use among children. 17. In a study by Armstrong, Reisinger, and Smith (2007), participants reported issues with wheelchair design, such as weak brakes and unavailable caster wheels. However, the adjustable wheelchair provided in the CIR Whirlwind project was generally well-received. 18. Active rehabilitation training programs for individuals with SCI improved mobility and independence, as indicated by increased SCI Independence Measure (SCIM) scores. 19. Wheelchair training based on the WHO 2008 Guidelines showed inconsistent findings regarding activities of daily living (ADLs) across different population groups. 20. The Dutch service delivery system, which included domestic and car adaptations and adaptive equipment provision, was found to improve functional health status when adults with SCI were satisfied with the services and procedures. 21. In a study by Leochico and Valera (2020), patients were asked to repeat demonstrations of exercises to ensure accurate understanding and safe execution. Necessary corrections and precautions were emphasized during these sessions.
